choices.title: Lambdoidal suture
choices.correct_explanation:
The lambdoidal suture (also called the lambdoid suture) is the fibrous joint that separates the occipital bone (specifically, its tabular portion) from the two parietal bones at the back of the skull. It is named after its resemblance to the Greek letter lambda (Λ).

Key features:

  • It is an immovable synarthrosis joint composed of dense connective tissue.
  • Plays a vital role in cranial molding during birth and allows brain growth in infancy.
  • Fusion of this suture typically occurs in adulthood, and premature fusion (craniosynostosis) may cause skull deformities.

Option a: Sagittal suture

The sagittal suture lies between the two parietal bones, running anterior to posterior along the midline of the skull. It does not involve the occipital bone.

  • Anatomical Note: The sagittal suture intersects the lambdoidal suture at the lambda, a cranial landmark.

Option b: Coronal suture

The coronal suture separates the frontal bone from the two parietal bones. It runs laterally across the top of the skull. It is unrelated to the occipital or tabular portions.

Option c: Frontal suture

The frontal (metopic) suture lies between the two halves of the frontal bone in infants and usually fuses by 6–8 years of age. It does not involve the parietal or occipital bones. The term “prontal” in the question appears to be a typographical error and is interpreted here as “frontal.”

Clinical Pearls:

  • Cranial sutures are important in pediatric assessment:
    • Premature closure of sutures → craniosynostosis (e.g., scaphocephaly with sagittal closure, plagiocephaly with lambdoidal closure).
    • Fontanelles (anterior, posterior) lie at suture junctions and help assess intracranial pressure and hydration status.
  • The lambdoidal suture is especially relevant in newborn skull assessments and in forensic and radiologic evaluations of head injuries.
